title: Development of a novel multiplex electrochemiluminescent-based immunoassay to aid enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli vaccine development and evaluations.
ehr_evidence: We used the serum and ALS (antibody in lymphocyte supernatant) samples from the volunteers vaccinated with ACE527 vaccine and placebo volunteers challenged with H10407 ETEC for validation of the multiplex ECL assay.
summary: A laboratory proof-of-concept study developing and validating an 8-plex electrochemiluminescent (MSD) immunoassay for measuring immune responses to ETEC antigens and comparing it with conventional ELISA using serum and ALS specimens from ACE527 vaccine volunteers.
key_findings: Intra-assay precision (CV) was below 20% (range 5.3%-18.1%) for all 8 antigens.
Inter-assay precision (CV) was below 20% (range 7.7%-17.9%) across 3 consecutive days.
Dilution linearity R² values were 90-100% for high titer and 75-90% for low titer serum.
Specificity: percent inhibition was over 60% for all antigens in the competitive inhibition assay.
No significant difference between ELISA and ECL for serum IgA except CS3 (p=.0087).
No significant difference for serum IgG except LTB IgG (p=.0200).
MSD platform was more sensitive than ELISA (max-to-min ratio 1434.62 vs 87.63).
captured_features: Antigen-specific antibody responses to CFA/I, CS1, CS2, CS3, CS5, CS6, LTA, LTB
Intra- and inter-assay coefficient of variation (CV%)
study_design: In vitro assay development and validation study (proof-of-concept comparison of multiplex ECL vs ELISA)
population: Healthy American adults who received the ACE527 ETEC vaccine or placebo and were challenged with ETEC H10407
exposure_domain: Vaccine/ETEC antigen-specific immune responses (colonization factors and heat-labile toxin antigens)
limitations: Small sample sizes (e.g., 10 serum samples for inter-assay precision).
ETEC antigens used are not commercially available, limiting reproducibility and standardization.
Relatively high MSD reader and plate costs and specialist printing requirements.
Study conducted in healthy adults, not the target pediatric/endemic population.
